newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican banking commission outlines revised rules.
newsitem.headline: Mexican banking commission outlines revised rules.

text.p: Mexico's National Banking and Securities Commission released revised rules on Friday that it said aim to bring its regulations more in line with the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP).
It said that up to December 1996, past-due loans contained only the unpaid principal of the loans, which meant that banks continued to accrue unpaid interest.

"Under the new regulation, the amount to be included under the past-due loans portfolio will be equal to the total amount outstanding and once the loan has been classified in such a manner, interest accrual will be discontinued," the Commission said in a news release.

Another significant change is that most market-traded financial assets must be disclosed on a mark-to-market basis, which should help to determine more clearly the real value of investments and thus the capital of the banks.
Fixed assets must also be periodically revalued according to inflation "and the inflationary profit or loss derived from monetary positions will be acknowledged," it said.
The new rules include changes on the registration and valuation of various debt instruments issued by the federal government, the United Mexican States (UMS).

UMS debt instruments that banks received in lieu of restructured federal government foreign debt in 1989 and 1990, as well as the Global Bonds received afterwards in exchange for these bonds "will be registered...at purchase cost under the category of securities held to maturity."
Other debt instruments must be market to market, it said.

In terms of bank's portfolios, interests that have been refinanced and accrued on past-due loans will be registered as principal, and loan loss provisions will be set up according to the results of quarterly grading of the loans portfolio.
"Past-due interests that were not refinanced must be fully provisioned," it said.
Loans restructured under federal government support programs will be registered under the current loans portfolio, it added.
Rules for the minimum level of loan loss provisions will be changed from 60 percent of past-due loans to 45 percent of the past-due loans portfolio.
"It should be underlined that as of September 1996, provisions already cover around 90 percent of past-due loans under former accounting principles," it said.
The Commission also spelled out transition steps on mortgage portfolios.
Banks will evaluate the viability of the past-due mortgage portfolios in order to allocate the loans under one of the two following options:
* Regulatory forbearance -- 35 percent of loans that are past-due under the new criteria must be fully provisioned.

* Rent-based schedule -- banks will have the option to allocate past-due loans whose recovery seems feasible. The maximum amount of loans entered into this scheme will be equal to 30 percent of the past-due mortgage portfolio.

Sixty-five percent of the total loan balance will earn the CPP (average cost of funds) interest rate, and the remaining 35 percent will accumulate the price variation of the UDI (an inflation-indexed unit of investment).
